questions.question: How do event capture, target, and bubbling work in the DOM?
questions.title: DOM event propagation
questions.direct_answer: A dispatched DOM event travels from the document side toward its target during capture, reaches the target, and then—when the event bubbles—travels back through the target's ancestors. Listeners can run in capture or bubble order, and the Event object reports both the original target and the current listener's element.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the three propagation phases and event properties are distinct.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Capture travels from ancestors toward the target.
The target phase runs at the element where the event originated.
Bubbling travels from the target through ancestors when the event bubbles.
event.target is the origin; event.currentTarget owns the running listener.
stopPropagation stops further travel but does not cancel the browser's default action.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- DOM event propagation gives ancestors a chance to observe an event around the element where it began. The path has a capture phase toward the target, a target phase, and usually a bubble phase back through ancestors.

- `addEventListener` uses the bubble phase by default. Passing `{ capture: true }` registers a listener for capture. For example, clicking a button inside a toolbar can first reach a document capture listener, then the button listener, and then the toolbar's bubble listener.

- `event.target` remains the node where the event originated, while `event.currentTarget` is the node whose listener is currently running. That difference lets one parent listener inspect which child was clicked.

- Propagation and default behaviour are separate. `stopPropagation` prevents the event from continuing along the path; `preventDefault` requests cancellation of a cancelable browser action such as link navigation. I avoid stopping propagation without a clear ownership boundary because it can silently break analytics, accessibility helpers, or other ancestor behaviour.

sections.title: One event can be observed along a path
sections.content: The browser computes a propagation path through the DOM tree. Listener phase and registration order determine which callbacks run; the target remains the source of the event throughout that journey.

sections.title: Not every event bubbles in the same way
sections.content:
Common events such as `click` bubble, while `focus` and `blur` do not; `focusin` and `focusout` are bubbling alternatives. Shadow DOM can retarget events so components preserve encapsulation, and the `composed` flag controls whether an event crosses a shadow boundary.

`stopImmediatePropagation` is stronger than `stopPropagation`: it also prevents later listeners on the same current target from running. It should be rare because it creates hidden coupling between otherwise independent listeners.

sections.title: Propagation path for a button click
sections.content:
CAPTURE: document → body → toolbar → button
TARGET:  button
BUBBLE:  button → toolbar → body → document

questions.question: What is event delegation, and when is it useful?
questions.title: Event delegation
questions.direct_answer: Event delegation places one listener on a stable ancestor and uses event propagation to handle matching descendants. It is useful for repeated or dynamically added elements because the ancestor listener remains valid, but its selector and containment checks must avoid treating unrelated nested elements as valid targets.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether delegation is derived from propagation rather than memorized as a trick.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Testing only event.target and failing when a nested icon is clicked.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Balancing dynamic coverage with event and selector boundaries.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Delegation depends on an event that reaches an ancestor.
Inspect event.target and find the intended descendant with closest.
Verify that the matched element belongs to the delegated container.
New matching descendants work without new listeners.
Use direct listeners when events do not propagate suitably or each item has distinct behaviour.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- Event delegation uses bubbling to replace many similar child listeners with one listener on a stable parent. When an event reaches the parent, the handler identifies the relevant child from `event.target`.

- For example, a todo list can listen once on the `ul` and use `event.target.closest("button[data-remove]")` to find a remove button. Items added later are automatically covered because the listener belongs to the list rather than to the original buttons.

- The match needs a boundary check. `closest` can walk beyond an inner subtree, and nested components may contain similar selectors, so the handler should verify that the result is contained by the expected delegation root. It should also use element semantics rather than fragile assumptions about the exact text or icon node clicked.

- Delegation is not always better. Some events do not bubble, high-frequency events may make broad matching expensive, and a small fixed control group may be clearer with direct listeners. I use it when descendants share behaviour and their membership changes over time.

sections.title: Move repeated routing logic to a stable ancestor
sections.content: The ancestor does not receive a different event. It observes the same propagated event and decides which descendant action, if any, owns it.

sections.title: Target normalization prevents nested-markup bugs
sections.content:
A button may contain an SVG or span, so `event.target` is not guaranteed to be the button. `closest` walks to the semantic action element. A containment check prevents a match from a nested or adjacent component from leaking into the wrong handler.

Keyboard activation of native buttons also produces click events, which makes delegation compatible with built-in accessibility. Replacing buttons with generic elements and custom key logic creates unnecessary work and inconsistent behaviour.

sections.title: One listener routes many descendants
sections.content:
click on icon inside button
event bubbles to list
closest(button[data-action])
validate containment → run action

questions.question: What is the difference between preventDefault and stopPropagation?
questions.title: Default actions and propagation
questions.direct_answer: preventDefault asks the browser not to perform a cancelable event's default action, such as following a link or submitting a form. stopPropagation prevents the event from continuing to other nodes on its propagation path. Neither method performs the other's job, and preventDefault has no effect when the event is not cancelable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether cancellation and propagation are treated as separate systems.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using stopPropagation when the goal is to prevent navigation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Knowing cancelable and passive listener boundaries.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: preventDefault cancels a cancelable browser default action.
stopPropagation stops travel to later nodes on the event path.
stopImmediatePropagation also stops later listeners on the same node.
defaultPrevented reports whether cancellation was requested.
A passive listener cannot call preventDefault successfully.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- `preventDefault` and `stopPropagation` control two independent parts of event processing. The default action is what the user agent would do after dispatch, while propagation determines which registered listeners can observe the event.

- For example, a form `submit` handler may call `preventDefault` to keep the browser from navigating while JavaScript validates and sends data. The submit event can still bubble to an ancestor listener unless propagation is stopped.

- Calling `stopPropagation` on a link click prevents ancestor listeners from seeing that click, but it does not stop navigation. `stopImmediatePropagation` additionally prevents later listeners on the current target. Both propagation methods can create surprising dependencies, so I use them only when an event must not cross a genuine component boundary.

- Cancellation also has limits. `preventDefault` works only for a cancelable event, and a listener registered as passive promises not to cancel it. I check `event.cancelable` or `defaultPrevented` when building reusable event code and prefer native element behaviour when no custom action is required.

sections.title: Dispatch and browser behaviour are separate
sections.content: Listeners run as the event is dispatched. If that event was cancelable and cancellation was requested, the associated default action is skipped; the event path itself is unchanged unless propagation is stopped.

sections.title: Passive listeners protect scrolling responsiveness
sections.content:
Touch and wheel listeners can delay scrolling if the browser must wait to learn whether they cancel it. A passive listener tells the browser that it will not call `preventDefault`, allowing scrolling to proceed. Attempting cancellation from such a listener is ignored and may produce a console warning.

Returning `false` from an `addEventListener` callback has no special effect. That older shorthand applies in some legacy event-handler APIs or libraries, so explicit methods are clearer.

sections.title: Two independent controls
sections.content:
| Method | Controls | Does not control |
|---|---|---|
| `preventDefault()` | Browser default action | Listener propagation |
| `stopPropagation()` | Later nodes on event path | Browser default action |
| `stopImmediatePropagation()` | Path and later same-node listeners | Browser default action |
